one_liner: dietlibc's in-place 3-way quicksort and binary search; a 2001 changelog claimed 2.3x and 6.1x fewer cycles than glibc.
what_it_does: These are the qsort and bsearch of diet libc, a small GPL libc for statically linked Linux programs. They keep the standard C signatures, so a program gets them by building with the diet wrapper (diet gcc ...) and linking the whole program statically against dietlibc.a, not by swapping one function into a glibc build. qsort sorts in place with no heap allocation; bsearch is a textbook halving search.
how_it_is_fast: The current qsort is the Sedgewick/Bentley 3-way partitioning quicksort from 'Quicksort is Optimal', with a random pivot drawn from a per-process Park-Miller generator (rand_i, seeded from the ELF AT_RANDOM bytes); keys equal to the pivot are gathered at the ends and swapped to the middle, so duplicate-heavy input finishes in near-linear time. It makes no malloc, syscall or first-call setup, which is the likeliest source of its 2001 win over glibc's merge sort (glibc 2.2's first large qsort call read /etc/mtab and /proc/meminfo to size its buffer, then malloc'd it). There is no insertion-sort cutoff, median-of-three or word-sized swap, so on random distinct keys it is not algorithmically faster: a Python port of lib/qsort.c made 15,814 comparator calls on 1000 random distinct keys (1.59 n log2 n), against 8,735 for a glibc-style top-down merge sort on the same data.
when_to_use: You already build a static Linux binary against dietlibc for size (initramfs tools, rescue or embedded utilities) and need a working qsort/bsearch at no extra cost.
Sorting must not touch the heap: dietlibc's qsort is in place and only uses the recursion stack, while glibc's current qsort mallocs a merge buffer once the array exceeds 1024 bytes.
Inputs with many equal keys: 3-way partitioning sorts 1000 identical ints in 2,000 comparisons in the Python port (6 recursion levels or fewer for 4 distinct values).
You want a short, readable 3-way quicksort to study or adapt (lib/qsort.c is 73 lines), and GPL-2.0-or-later is acceptable.
when_not_to_use: Speed-critical sorting with a function-pointer comparator: about 1.8x more comparator calls than a merge sort on random distinct keys (Python port), byte-by-byte swaps, and the x86_64 build uses -Os; nothing shows it beating a current glibc.
You need a stable sort: it is an unstable quicksort.
Untrusted or adversarial input with tight stack limits: there is no recursion-depth bound and it recurses into both partitions, so worst-case stack depth is O(n).

You link prebuilt libraries compiled against glibc headers, need shared libraries, or target anything but Linux: the FAQ says glibc-compiled libraries fail to link (missing __ctype_b), shared libraries are experimental, and FreeBSD/Solaris/Windows ports are refused.
Proprietary binaries: the libc is GPL-2.0-or-later and statically linked, so distributed binaries carry GPL obligations (the FAQ only promises not to sue over BSD programs with public source).

integration.dependencies: none (Linux syscalls only); qsort.c also needs rand_i.c, which uses getauxval(AT_RANDOM) and rand_r
integration.min_toolchain: GCC (FAQ: compiling dietlibc with another compiler is not supported; CHANGES 0.34 adds clang support with larger code and no cross-compiling); bsearch.c uses GNU void-pointer arithmetic
integration.platforms: Linux only: i386, x86_64, arm, aarch64, mips, ppc/ppc64, sparc/sparc64, s390, alpha, parisc, ia64 per the Makefile
integration.thread_safety: bsearch is stateless; qsort is reentrant except that rand_i keeps an unsynchronized static seed, a data race under concurrent qsort calls that only perturbs pivot choice
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same qsort/bsearch signatures, but you get them only by linking the whole program statically against dietlibc; copying lib/qsort.c alone needs rand_i and puts the file under GPL-2.0-or-later

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the numbers: CHANGES gives no method, and the closest harness is the scratch t.c in the same 2001 commit (344deb2), which times one rdtsc-bracketed qsort and one bsearch per run (SIZE is 100000 there, not the 1000 quoted). Its warm-up qsort(array,2,...) is 8 bytes, which glibc 2.2's msort.c sorts on an alloca buffer, so the timed glibc call is the first to take the 1024-byte-or-larger path: sysconf(_SC_PHYS_PAGES), which in glibc 2.2 parses /etc/mtab and /proc/meminfo through stdio, then malloc/free of the merge buffer. bsearch gets no warm-up, so glibc's 3,352 cycles for one lookup probably include first-call costs (cold cache, and lazy PLT binding if glibc was linked dynamically, which is not stated). The repo's later timing test, test/qsort.c, is no better: its string comparator loops while (l=(*A-*B)), an inverted condition, so it always returns 0 (every key compares equal, which a 3-way quicksort finishes in one pass) and its 'not sorted' check can never fire.

The measured 2001 qsort never advances its left scan past a key equal to the pivot, so it goes quadratic with O(n) recursion depth on all-equal or few-distinct input (Python port: 1,001,948 comparisons and depth 993 for 1000 equal ints; 4,029,021 comparisons for 4000 ints with 4 distinct values). It was replaced on 2003-11-02 ('write new qsort that does not fail so').

The measured 2001 bsearch shrinks the window by num instead of num+1 when it moves right, so probes can land past the end of the array: it reads out of bounds and can miss keys that are present, not only the last one (Python port: sizes 1 to 199 read past the end for 137 sizes; with n=13 it misses index 11 when the word past the end is smaller than the key), and with nmemb 0 it still reads base[0]. CHANGES records bsearch fixes in 0.10, 0.11, 0.13 ('didn't find the very last element') and 0.15.

From 'faster qsort' (2006-08-16, the 0.31 changelog line) until commit 635fb76 (2012-08-27, 'two fixes by Enrico Scholz') the pivot was the rightmost element, quadratic with recursion depth n on sorted or reversed input (Python port: 501,498 comparisons for 1000 sorted ints), so 0.31/0.32-era packages carry it. From 2012 to 2019-01-29 the random pivot called rand(), which advanced the program's own rand() sequence, until rand_i replaced it (CHANGES 0.35).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Only when the program is already built against dietlibc for binary size. For speed, swenson/sort (typed C macros, about 2.2x libc qsort on 10,000 int64 in its README) or pdqsort and crumsort are measured alternatives; dietlibc's qsort has no current evidence of beating anything.
verified_claims_summary: The only numbers are one changelog line from 2001 (section 0.7.3, later 0.8): on 1000 random ints, glibc's qsort took 679,414 cycles against dietlibc's 300,010, and one bsearch took 3,352 against 553 cycles. No compiler, flags, CPU or glibc version is given, the probable harness times a single call of each, and both measured routines were later rewritten after correctness and robustness fixes.
status_note: The ensc git-cvs mirror is archived (2023-09-05, last commit 2019-03-18; upstream is CVS at cvs.fefe.de) and the code is usable as part of dietlibc under GPL-2.0-or-later, but the benchmarked qsort and bsearch are gone and the 2.3x/6.1x figures are historical and probably not reproducible against current glibc, whose qsort is now a merge sort with a heapsort fallback.
